questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Dimensions of Food Security' refers to.
questions.a: The multi-faceted framework of food security encompassing its physical availability, economic and physical accessibility, and financial affordability to all individuals.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Dimensions of Food Security'.
questions.a: Food security requires food to be available, reachable, and affordable for everyone without barriers.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Dimensions of Food Security' taught, and from which source text?

questions.a: 2 units

Use the method 'Total Foodgrain Availability Calculation'. Work with: exports = 4, imports = 15, production = 10. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of total_availability.
questions.a: 21 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Total Foodgrain Availability Calculation' refers to.
questions.a: The quantitative measurement of the net amount of foodgrains available in a region or country, calculated by adding domestic production and imports, and subtracting exports.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Total Foodgrain Availability Calculation'.
questions.a: Net food availability is the sum of domestic output and net trade.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Total Foodgrain Availability Calculation', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: total_availability = production + imports - exports

concepts.title: Impact of Natural Calamity on Food Security

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Impact of Natural Calamity on Food Security' refers to.
questions.a: The process by which natural disasters disrupt agricultural production, leading to food shortages, price inflation, and potential starvation or famine.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Impact of Natural Calamity on Food Security'.
questions.a: Calamities decrease food production, driving up prices and making food unaffordable for the poorest.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Impact of Natural Calamity on Food Security' taught, and from which source text?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Food Insecure Groups' refers to.
questions.a: Identification of social and economic segments of the population that are highly vulnerable to nutritional and food deprivation.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Food Insecure Groups'.
questions.a: Landless laborers, traditional artisans, casual urban workers, and marginalized social groups face the highest risk of food insecurity.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Food Insecure Groups' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Who are food-insecure? (source: iess204.txt lines 110-145)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Chronic vs Seasonal Hunger' refers to.
questions.a: Distinguishing between persistent, long-term hunger due to low income (chronic) and cyclical hunger linked to agricultural or casual labor patterns (seasonal).

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Chronic vs Seasonal Hunger'.
questions.a: Chronic hunger stems from structural poverty, while seasonal hunger is tied to periodic employment cycles.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Chronic vs Seasonal Hunger' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Who are food-insecure? (source: iess204.txt lines 175-205)

concepts.title: Buffer Stock and Minimum Support Price

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Buffer Stock and Minimum Support Price' refers to.
questions.a: The government mechanism of procuring foodgrains (wheat and rice) from surplus states at a pre-announced price (MSP) to maintain security reserves.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Buffer Stock and Minimum Support Price'.
questions.a: MSP incentivizes farmers to produce, while buffer stocks ensure grain availability for distribution during shortages.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Buffer Stock and Minimum Support Price' taught, and from which source text?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Public Distribution System (PDS)' refers to.
questions.a: The system through which the government distributes subsidized foodgrains and essential commodities to the poor via a network of fair price shops.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Public Distribution System (PDS)'.
questions.a: PDS acts as a price-stabilizing and food-distributing network of ration shops.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Public Distribution System (PDS)' taught, and from which source text?

questions.a: 6900 persons

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'National Food Security Act (NFSA) Coverage' refers to.
questions.a: The legal framework providing subsidized foodgrains to eligible households, covering specified percentages of rural and urban populations.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'National Food Security Act (NFSA) Coverage'.
questions.a: NFSA 2013 legally guarantees food security to 75% of rural and 50% of urban populations.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'National Food Security Act (NFSA) Coverage', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: eligible_population = (rural_population * 0.75) + (urban_population * 0.50)

concepts.title: Role of Cooperatives in Food Security

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Role of Cooperatives in Food Security' refers to.
questions.a: The contribution of cooperative societies and non-governmental networks in distributing essential food items at controlled, affordable rates.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Role of Cooperatives in Food Security'.
questions.a: Cooperatives like Amul, Mother Dairy, and grain banks run by NGOs provide alternative, reliable channels for food security.
